# Jubilees — Reader's Guide
**Guide:** HESED | **Category:** Pseudepigrapha (PS)

---

## At a Glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attribution** | Moses (dictated by the Angel of the Presence on Sinai) |
| **Actual Composition** | c. 160–150 BCE |
| **Language** | Ge'ez (Ethiopic); Hebrew fragments at Qumran (4QJub^a–b and others) |
| **Audience** | Jewish priestly and scribal circles concerned with calendar, law, and national identity |
| **Genre** | Rewritten Bible — retelling of Genesis through Exodus 20 with halakhic expansion and jubilee chronology |
| **Length** | 50 chapters |
| **In One Sentence** | God dictates to Moses the true version of history from creation to Sinai, organized by jubilee cycles, emphasizing the 364-day solar calendar, circumcision, Sabbath, and Israel's eternal election against the threat of assimilation and apostasy. |

---

## Sections Overview

Jubilees follows the narrative arc of Genesis and the early chapters of Exodus almost continuously, but it restructures everything within a chronological grid of jubilees (49-year cycles of seven "weeks" of years). The entire sweep of sacred history from creation to Sinai fits into exactly 50 jubilees.

### Prologue and Sinai Frame (1:1–29)
The book opens on Sinai. Moses has been on the mountain for forty days. God commands the Angel of the Presence to dictate to Moses "the account of the division of all the years of eternity" — the true, hidden history that the public text of the Torah only partially reveals. Chapter 1 also includes a remarkable prophecy of Israel's future apostasy, exile, and eventual restoration — a periodization of national history delivered before the entry into Canaan.

### Creation and the Antediluvian World (2:1–7:39)
The creation account (ch. 2) establishes the 364-day solar calendar as the cosmic norm — God built the week into the fabric of creation, and the luminaries were appointed to govern a solar year of exactly 52 weeks (4 × 91 days). Sabbath observance is stressed as unique to Israel among the nations, a covenant sign shared between God and his people and the angels of the presence.

The antediluvian genealogies introduce a persistent theme: the heavenly tablets contain every person's destiny, and history unfolds according to their decrees. The descent of the Watchers (ch. 4–5) is retold more tersely than in 1 Enoch, but Jubilees adds that the demons (spirits of the dead Nephilim) were permitted to afflict humanity — nine-tenths were bound by God, but one-tenth remained free to mislead Israel, operating under the command of Mastema.

### Noah and the Covenant (6:1–10:36)
Noah's flood and the covenant of the rainbow are retold with explicit legal content. The law against eating blood is codified here as an eternal statute. Chapter 6 is pivotal: Noah and his sons celebrate the Festival of Weeks (Shavuot) after the flood — establishing that this feast was ordained before Sinai, written on the heavenly tablets. The reader begins to see Jubilees' main theological move: every festival, every law, was already known to the righteous of earlier ages.

The Table of Nations (ch. 8–9) is restructured around Noah's division of the earth among his three sons, with precise geographical assignments given to Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The author uses this framework to argue that the land of Canaan rightfully belongs to Shem's portion — and that the Canaanites are squatters on land that was never theirs.

### Abraham (11:1–23:10)
This is the longest section of the book and its theological heart. Abram's story is retold with major expansions not found in Genesis:

- **Abram's youth** (ch. 11–12): Abram is a monotheist from childhood who argues with his father Terah against idol worship and personally discovers the true God by observing the heavens. He prays in Hebrew — the "language of creation" — which had ceased to be spoken by other peoples at Babel.
- **The covenant and its trials** (ch. 14–18): The covenant ceremonies of Genesis 15 and 17 are retold and given precise jubilee dates. Circumcision is absolute — any male who is not circumcised on the eighth day has broken the covenant irreparably. The binding of Isaac (ch. 18) is prefaced by a scene in heaven where Mastema challenges God to test Abraham, closely paralleling the Job prologue.
- **Abraham's farewell** (ch. 19–22): Abraham delivers extended blessings and legal instructions to his descendants before his death — including Jubilees' most explicit condemnation of intermarriage with Gentiles and of abandoning circumcision.

### Jacob and His Sons (25:1–46:16)
The Jacob cycle is retold with characteristic expansions. Rebecca delivers legal instruction to Jacob (ch. 25) and exhorts him never to marry a Canaanite woman — an implicit polemic against intermarriage. The story of Dinah and Shechem (ch. 30) becomes a platform for the absolute prohibition of intermarriage: Simeon and Levi are praised (contra Genesis 34 where Jacob rebukes them), and any Israelite man who gives his daughter to a Gentile, or any Israelite woman who lies with a Gentile man, is to be put to death, since they have defiled Israel's holy seed.

Jacob, like Abraham, observes the festivals before Sinai. He celebrates Sukkot (ch. 16), Shavuot (ch. 44), and other festivals in their proper times — confirming that the laws of Moses were the laws of the patriarchs. The Joseph story (ch. 34, 40–46) is abbreviated; Jubilees is not interested in Joseph as a narrative hero but as a link in the genealogical-legal chain.

### Levi and the Priestly Line (30:18–32:15)
A substantial expansion is devoted to Levi's divine appointment as priest. Jacob's vision of Levi (ch. 32) confirms the Levitical priesthood as ordained before the establishment of the Aaronic order. This section has close affinities with the Aramaic Levi Document found at Qumran — both texts reflect a tradition of Levi as the founding priestly patriarch.

### Moses and the Exodus Prologue (46:1–50:13)
The final section covers the story of Israel in Egypt, the plagues, the Passover, and the journey to Sinai. The Passover is presented with detailed legal requirements (ch. 49) going beyond Exodus — it must be observed in the sanctuary, it cannot be offered by non-priests, and its timing must follow the solar calendar. The book closes (ch. 50) with Sabbath law: its violation is punishable by death, and it is the eternal sign of Israel's covenant holiness. The final verse returns to the Sinai frame: this is the account Moses was commanded to write.

---

## The World Behind the Text

Jubilees was composed during one of the most turbulent periods in Jewish history. In 167 BCE, the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes entered Jerusalem, desecrated the temple, outlawed circumcision and Sabbath observance, and attempted to force Jews to assimilate into Hellenistic culture. The Maccabean revolt (167–160 BCE) drove out the Seleucids and restored Jewish independence under the Hasmoneans — but the crisis did not end there.

For priestly circles in particular, the threat of Hellenization was not just political but liturgical. The Jerusalem temple establishment had, in the years before Antiochus, been deeply compromised by Hellenizing high priests (Jason, Menelaus) who purchased the priesthood, established a gymnasium next to the temple, and encouraged Jews to abandon their distinctive practices. The calendar was a flashpoint: the traditional lunar calendar used in the temple was increasingly viewed by some as the calendar of compromise, while the 364-day solar calendar — which produced a fixed, invariant festival schedule — was promoted as the true, heavenly calendar that God had ordained from creation.

Jubilees addresses all of these concerns simultaneously. By placing the solar calendar in creation week itself, by tracing circumcision, Sabbath, and the festivals back to the patriarchs, and by framing intermarriage as equivalent to apostasy, the book argues that the Torah is not a recent Mosaic invention but the eternal law written on heavenly tablets — the law that created order has always required.

The book was composed in Hebrew (as the Qumran fragments confirm) and was probably the product of priestly-scribal circles aligned with or proto-Qumranian in orientation. Whether Jubilees preceded the Qumran community's founding, or was composed within it, remains debated — but the ideological overlap is extensive.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

Jubilees has a clear and urgent purpose: **to demonstrate that the law given at Sinai is not new**. It is the eternal law written on the heavenly tablets before creation, which righteous people have always known and always obeyed.

This argument accomplishes several things at once:

**Against Hellenization:** If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob already observed circumcision, Sabbath, and the festivals — not because Moses commanded them but because the heavenly tablets decreed them — then abandoning these practices is not adaptation to a new world but betrayal of the deepest structure of reality.

**For the solar calendar:** If God built a 364-day solar year into creation itself, and if Noah celebrated Shavuot on the correct solar date, then the lunar calendar used in Jerusalem is wrong by definition. Calendar is not liturgical bureaucracy; it is cosmic obedience.

**Against intermarriage:** The patriarchal narratives are reread to make endogamy (marriage within Israel) an absolute, eternal requirement. This is not Ezra's post-exilic innovation — it was already the law of heaven that Rebekah knew and Jacob obeyed.

**For Levitical priestly authority:** The Levitical priesthood is traced back before Aaron, before Moses, to Levi himself — establishing its legitimacy independently of Sinai and therefore beyond the reach of royal or political manipulation.

---

## How to Read This Book

**Know Genesis and Exodus first.** Jubilees is not an independent narrative — it is a rewriting of existing scripture. The reader is expected to know what the Genesis text says and to notice where Jubilees expands, changes, or adds. When Jubilees omits something, that is also significant (the morally complex episodes tend to be cleaned up or excised).

**Track the jubilee dates.** Every major event is assigned to a specific year of a specific week of a specific jubilee. These numbers are not decorative — they are theological claims. The precision asserts that history is not random; it unfolds according to heavenly reckoning. The chronological grid also allows the author to calculate forward to the reader's own time, implying that the present moment falls at a calculable point in the divine plan.

**Watch for the heavenly tablets.** This phrase appears throughout the book as the ultimate source of law and destiny. The heavenly tablets are prior to Scripture; Moses is writing down what is already inscribed there. This is the book's theory of revelation: Torah is the earthly transcript of an eternal heavenly document.

**Pay attention to what gets added.** The original Genesis text does not tell us what Abram did as a child, what language he prayed in, or how he reasoned to monotheism. Jubilees invents all of this. These additions reveal what the author thought was missing from the public text and what he needed his audience to believe about their founding father.

**The legal interpolations are the point.** At first reading, the long speeches of Abraham, Rebecca, and Jacob about avoiding Gentile women or keeping the Passover exactly right may feel like interruptions of the narrative. They are not interruptions — they are the reason the narrative exists. The story is the vehicle for the law.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

### With Genesis and Exodus
Jubilees covers Genesis 1 through Exodus 20 almost completely, with expansions, omissions, and revisions. It is best understood as an authoritative commentary on those texts dressed as a revelation superior to them — God is not explaining what Moses wrote; Moses is writing down what God is revealing fresh.

### With 1 Enoch
The two books share a common world. Both preserve the Watchers tradition (fallen angels, Nephilim, demonic spirits). Both insist on the 364-day solar calendar — the Astronomical Book of 1 Enoch and Jubilees chapter 6 are likely drawing on a common priestly calendar tradition. Mastema in Jubilees is closely related to Azazel and the leading Watchers in 1 Enoch. These books were almost certainly produced in overlapping or related circles.

### With the Dead Sea Scrolls
No book found at Qumran outside the Hebrew Bible is cited as authoritative as often as Jubilees. The Damascus Document (CD 16:3–4) explicitly references "the Book of the Divisions of the Times according to their Jubilees and their Weeks" — i.e., Jubilees — as a source of law. Multiple Hebrew manuscripts of Jubilees (4QJub^a, 4QJub^b, 4QJub^c, 4QJub^d, 4QJub^e, and others) were found in Caves 1–4. The Qumran community followed the 364-day solar calendar that Jubilees mandates. For the people who wrote the Dead Sea Scrolls, Jubilees was Scripture.

### With the Aramaic Levi Document and Testament of Levi
The extended focus on Levi's divine appointment in Jubilees 30–32 overlaps with the Aramaic Levi Document (found at Qumran and in the Cairo Geniza) and the later Testament of Levi (part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs). All three texts reflect a tradition of Levi as the founding priestly figure. The relationship between these documents — which came first, which depends on which — is one of the productive open questions in Second Temple studies.

### With the New Testament
Jubilees is not quoted in the New Testament, but its world is everywhere in the background:
- The **Mastema tradition** shapes how the NT depicts Satan as the adversary who challenges God's elect.
- The **heavenly tablets** concept underlies language in Revelation about the "book of life."
- Paul's argument in Galatians 3 that Abraham was justified before circumcision — and that the law came 430 years after the promise — is a counter-argument to precisely the kind of claim Jubilees makes about Abraham's pre-Sinaitic law-observance.
- Jesus' saying that the Sabbath was made for man (Mark 2:27) resonates against Jubilees' claim that Sabbath was made exclusively for Israel.

### With the Ethiopian Orthodox Canon
Like 1 Enoch, Jubilees is canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, where it is called *Kufale* ("divisions" or "portions") — a direct translation of the Greek title *ta diaireseis* ("the divisions of times"). Ethiopian tradition preserves the only complete text. The Ge'ez version is a translation from Greek, which was itself translated from the Hebrew original.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

1. **The jubilee chronology is a calculation device, not mere record-keeping.** A jubilee is 49 years (7 × 7); the "jubilee of jubilees" — 49 × 49 = 2,401 years — plays a structuring role in some reconstructions. The author assigns creation to a precise year and counts forward, placing the Sinai revelation at the end of exactly 50 jubilees (2,450 years). This allows ancient readers to locate themselves in sacred history. Some scholars have argued the author was counting forward to the Maccabean period, implying that his readers were living at a pivotal jubilee juncture.

2. **The 364-day calendar is a theological claim, not an astronomical error.** The author knew perfectly well that the tropical solar year is approximately 365.25 days. The 364-day year — divisible evenly by 4 and by 7 — was chosen because it produces a perfectly regular festival calendar: every year, every festival falls on exactly the same day of the week. No intercalation is needed; no priestly calculation can shift a festival from its proper day. This was a polemic against the Jerusalem temple establishment, whose lunar (and lunisolar) calendar the author regarded as both theologically incorrect and politically manipulable.

3. **Mastema is not simply "the devil."** He is a specific figure — the chief of the evil spirits (the demons born from the dead Nephilim) — who serves an ambiguous function. God permits him to retain one-tenth of his spirits to "do evil and rule over the children of men" (10:8–9). Mastema is behind Pharaoh's hardened heart, behind the temptation of Abraham at the binding of Isaac, behind the attack on Moses before the Exodus (a scene derived from Exod 4:24–26). He is simultaneously God's adversary and God's instrument of testing — a Satan figure who operates within divinely sanctioned limits.

4. **The patriarchs already kept the festivals — and the book means this literally.** Noah celebrates the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot) after the flood (6:17). Abraham celebrates Sukkot (Booths) at Beersheba (16:20–31). Jacob celebrates the Feast of First Fruits and Sukkot (44:1–8). These are not symbolic or typological readings; Jubilees is asserting that the festivals were observed historically, before Moses, because they are written on the heavenly tablets. The Sinai revelation did not create the law; it published it.

5. **Jubilees' treatment of the Dinah episode is a deliberate reinterpretation.** Genesis 34 ends ambiguously — Simeon and Levi kill the Shechemites, and Jacob rebukes them: "You have troubled me." Jubilees 30 completely reverses this verdict. Simeon and Levi acted rightly; Jacob was wrong to rebuke them. Any Israelite man who gives his daughter to a Gentile must die; any Israelite woman who has sexual relations with a Gentile must die; their blood is on their own hands. This is among the harshest expressions of ethnic-religious exclusivism in Second Temple Jewish literature, and it was almost certainly written in response to Hellenizing intermarriage in the author's own community.

6. **The book recasts Hebrew as the sacred language of creation and election.** In the aftermath of Babel (ch. 12), humanity forgot Hebrew and began to speak "the tongue of the Gentiles." Abram alone prayed to God in Hebrew, which the author calls "the language of creation." God commands an angel to teach Abraham to read and write Hebrew again. This is a claim that Israel's language is not just ancient but cosmically privileged — and an implicit polemic against Jews who were transacting their religious life in Greek.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

Jubilees is **canonical scripture** in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Church, where it has been part of the biblical collection for over fifteen hundred years. For these communities, it is simply part of the Bible.

For Western Christianity and Rabbinic Judaism, its exclusion resulted from a convergence of factors:

**The Hebrew original was lost.** Outside Qumran (where the scrolls were sealed in the first century CE and not rediscovered until 1947), the Hebrew text disappeared. The Greek translation circulated in late antiquity but was not widely copied. The complete text survived only in Ge'ez, which remained inaccessible to European scholarship until the nineteenth century.

**Its legal agenda was too specific.** The insistence on the 364-day solar calendar, the absolute prohibition on intermarriage, and the harshness of its purity codes placed it outside the mainstream of both Pharisaic Judaism (which eventually became Rabbinic Judaism) and early Christianity. The Pharisees followed the lunar calendar; the early church was explicitly opening covenant membership to Gentiles.

**Pseudepigraphy was eventually disqualifying.** As both Jewish and Christian communities developed canons, the attribution of revelation to a figure who could not have written it — Moses dictating what the Angel of the Presence said — became a reason for exclusion rather than a literary convention to be accepted.

**At Qumran it was authoritative; at Jamnia it was not.** The Qumran community, which was probably related to the circles that produced Jubilees, was destroyed in 68 CE. The Pharisaic tradition that survived the destruction of Jerusalem and shaped Rabbinic Judaism had no special investment in Jubilees.

The first complete European translation from Ge'ez was made by August Dillmann in German in 1850–1851. The first English translation by Robert Henry Charles appeared in 1895. The Qumran discoveries (1947 onward) proved beyond doubt that Jubilees was composed in Hebrew and circulated widely in pre-Christian Jewish Palestine.

---

## Timeline

| Date (approx.) | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 400–200 BCE | Underlying calendar and legal traditions take shape in priestly circles |
| c. 175–167 BCE | Maccabean crisis: Antiochus IV Epiphanes desecrates the temple; circumcision and Sabbath outlawed |
| c. 160–150 BCE | Jubilees composed in Hebrew, probably in priestly-scribal circles aligned with proto-Qumranian movement |
| c. 150–100 BCE | Book circulates in Hebrew; Qumran community copies made (4QJub^a–f and others) |
| c. 100 BCE – 68 CE | Qumran copies in active use; Damascus Document cites Jubilees as authoritative |
| 68 CE | Qumran destroyed by Romans; Hebrew copies sealed in caves |
| c. 2nd–3rd c. CE | Greek translation circulates; patristic writers (Justin, Origen, Epiphanius) reference it |
| c. 4th–6th c. CE | Translated into Ge'ez; becomes part of Ethiopian Orthodox biblical canon (*Kufale*) |
| c. 4th–5th c. CE | Excluded from Western Latin canon; Greek text gradually lost |
| 1844–1848 CE | Antoine d'Abbadie brings Ge'ez manuscripts from Ethiopia; scholarly access opens |
| 1850–1851 CE | August Dillmann publishes first critical edition and German translation from Ge'ez |
| 1895 CE | R.H. Charles publishes first English translation |
| 1947–1956 CE | Hebrew fragments discovered at Qumran (Caves 1–4), confirming Hebrew original |
| 1989 CE | James VanderKam publishes critical edition of Ge'ez text and new English translation (CSCO) |
| 2001 CE | Hebrew fragments fully published in *Discoveries in the Judaean Desert* (DJD 13) |

---

*HESED notes: Jubilees is among the most important books for understanding the religious world that produced both the Dead Sea Scrolls and early Christianity. Its insistence that the law is eternal and pre-Sinaitic, its 364-day solar calendar, and its fierce protectiveness of Israelite identity mark it as a document born of crisis — but its theological ambition is considerable. Readers coming from the 1 Enoch guide will immediately recognize shared traditions; readers coming from the Hebrew Bible will recognize the same stories told with a sharper and more anxious edge.*
